newsitem.title: USA: "Go away" say Cuban exiles to Castro.
newsitem.headline: "Go away" say Cuban exiles to Castro.

text.p: As Cuban President Fidel Castro celebrated his 71st birthday on Wednesday, Cuban exiles in Miami said they hoped it would be his last in power.
The leading U.S. Cuban exile group sent out a message saying it supported any action to oust Castro, one of the world's longest-serving leaders.

"The Cuban American National Foundation, aware of its responsibility to the Cuban people, backs without ambiguity or misgiving whatever denunciation, confrontation or act of internal rebellion leads to the expulsion of Fidel and (his brother) Raul Castro from power and finally to peace and well-being for our people," it said in a full-page statement in the Spanish-language Nuevo Herald newspaper.
The CANF also speculated that members of Cuba's armed forces could have been behind a recent spate of hotel bombings on the island.

The bomb attacks, which have wounded three people and caused minor damage, were carried out by people with the knowledge, contacts and discipline to avoid detection by Cuban security forces, the statement said.
"These factors point to highly organized elements in the country, perhaps within the armed forces."
The CANF, led by multimillionaire businessman Jorge Mas Canosa, is the most powerful anti-Castro group and wields great influence over U.S. policy.
Exiles in Miami noted Castro's birthday in radio shows but with little fanfare.
"The only birthday wish I have for him is that he goes away and the Cuban people can be free," said Ninoska Perez, who presents a popular Spanish-language show.

Congressman Lincoln Diaz-Balart, whose birthday was also on Wednesday, told the Sun-Sentinel: "I think that Castro is an unburied corpse. The only question is how much disease he can spread before he's buried."
Despite the bomb attacks, a U.S. embargo and the fervent wishes of the exiles, there is little sign Castro will relinquish power soon.
Along 8th Street, the heart of Miami's Cuban community, gossip dwells on the health of the man who has ruled Cuba since the 1959 revolution that toppled dictator Fulgencio Batista.
"You can seen he doesn't look well," Perez said.

Speculation that Castro may be ill has been fueled by the facts that he has not made a public speech since early April and that at some recent public appearances he has looked tired. He has, however, periodically lapsed into silence in the past.
In Cuba, Castro's birthday celebrations were expected to be low-key, in keeping with traditional official discretion about his private life.
